To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

boosting at 7 weeks after primary immunizations with a recombinantdmdB Salmonella enterica serotype Typhimurioral vaccine strain resulted in a significantly lower response than boosting at 14 or 21 weeks after primary immunizaiton.

boosting at 7 weeks following immunization with the recombinantly expressed HagB resulted in reduced serum IgG antibody responses and that deliberate preimmunization with the carrier alone resulted in reduced serum antibody responses at 14 but not 7 weeks following primary immunization.

boosting with recombinant Salmonella strains is best done at a point in time when the primary immune response is waning, that boosting with Salmonella carrier alone does not affect subsequent responses to the recombinant vaccine, and that preexisting immunity to the Salmonellacarrier strain can affect the mucosal and humoral immune response.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
deliberate preimmunization with the carrier did not significantly affect the mucosal or systemic immune responses to the HagB antigen.
the immune response of the host to the carrier strain does not significantly affect the immune responses to the foreign gene product expressed by the Salmonella carrier.
the presence of preexisting immunity to the Salmonellacarrier strain has a limited effect on subsequent immune responses to the recombinant vaccine strain.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the primary immune response to the recombinant Salmonella strain was robust and that the recall response to the recomminant strain was generally not affected by preexisting immunity to the carrier.

the immune response to the recombinant antigen is dependent on the presence of a preexisting immune response to the carrier strain and that this response is not necessarily reflected in the level of Salmonella colonization.

a primary response was obtained with a single dose of recombinant Salmonella, but that boosting was required for an optimal response, and that the timing of boosting and the preimmunization status of the animal had a significant effect on the response to the recombinant antigen.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Salmonella carrier immunization does not appear to affect the immune response to a recombinant strain expressing a foreign antigen.
Salmonella-based vectors may have the ability to elicit a strong immune response even in the face of prior Salmonella-specific immunity.
boosting of oral immunizations with recombinant salmonellae is best performed at 14 weeks or later.
